old: Two pricing shapes are kept in one record because they are the same product and the difference is the point: the per-proxy plan's unlimited bandwidth is bounded by a 50 GB fair-use threshold, which is the number that matters at 45 GB a month, and splitting the record would hide that. Candidates for why the product fails, tested in order: (1) the identity gate, confirmed by the help page sentence on Tier 1 verification before first use; (2) the volume ceiling, real but not disqualifying at 45 GB, since one proxy covers the workload with 5 GB of headroom; (3) the exits being synthetic, refuted for 172.58.14.102, which RIPE aligns to AS21928 T-Mobile USA, and confirmed only for the graphic's 100.64.12.7, which sits in RFC 6598 shared space with no ASN. The address finding rests on one lookup per address on 2026-10-24, taken from RIPE Stat's prefix-overview rather than from a request through an issued endpoint; a session through an approved account would settle it and nothing else available here would. A third-party comparison blog (caproxy, 2025-12-08) claims a free version covering up to 5 ports; no vendor page read here confirms it, so free_tier records what the vendor prices and nothing more, and a vendor page naming a free plan would move it. The interface token is unknown because none of the cited pages records the protocol, and because scripts/dossier/schema.json's interface enum has no socks5, http-proxy, api or web-ui value for a record to use; validate.py rejects those tokens, so the protocol belongs in interface_detail until the enum is extended.

This resolves the exit sample that the record published in its marketing graphic; the registration class of an address issued to a buyer is unverified: behind an approved account.

old: Candidates for why the page yields no readable price, tested rather than assumed. (1) The form is rendered client-side: confirmed, the served HTML carries 'Price for 1 IP : $0' and the select elements hold ObjectId values, so the number is computed after hydration. (2) The $0.98 is a marketing floor reachable only at volume: consistent with the same page's 'Get a better per-IP rate with larger volumes or longer terms' and with its structured-data 'Minimum Price' of $3/IP, so the entry price at 1 IP is probably $3 and the $0.98 is a large-quantity rate — plausible, not established. (3) A WAF or geo-block was suppressing the price: refuted, the page returned 200 with the full article, the FAQ and the JSON-LD. Reading the ladder from https://proxy-seller.com/price/ was tried and ruled out: that page's ISP tab is drawn client-side and the table in the served HTML is the Residential per-GB ladder. What would settle the price: an account plus an API key, then orderCalcIsp across the 1w to 12mo periods at quantity 1, or simply the checkout for 1 IP for 1 week; the SDK makes this a scripted read rather than a browser session. What would settle the diversity claim, which no price settles: one 1-IP order, then ip.pkgforge.dev/json and RIPE prefix-overview on the delivered address, plus a second and third IP to see whether they land in different /24s and different ASNs. The vendor names carriers (AT&T, Windstream, Frontier) and the survey names the AS numbers; I verified the numbers against RIPE as-overview and they agree with the carrier names, but the mapping from those ASNs to the addresses actually delivered is the vendor's claim and is untested here — the RIPE lookups are one per ASN on one date, and nothing else in this record rests on a single sample. The Fair Usage Policy contradicts the marketing card and both are quoted rather than reconciled: 'Traffic is uncapped at any volume' against '100 GB of traffic by default' per IP, with no period stated and no way to buy traffic without buying an IP, which is why egress.metered is true while binding stays none at 45 GB a month. 'paid-only' was considered and rejected: the corpus's target includes cheapest-paid capacity, the minimum purchase is a single IP for a week, and the caveat belongs to the unverified price and the untested registration class rather than to the absence of a free tier. The schema's interface enum carries no proxy token, so interface holds 'rest' for the documented JSON API and the proxy protocols are in interface_detail, the shape dossier/storage/proxyrack-unlimited-residential.json already uses for a SOCKS5 product; the topic's own token list (socks5, http-proxy, api, web-ui) is not in schema.json and would fail the gate.
